title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
shortDefinition: An AI architecture that retrieves relevant external information before generating a response with a language model.
definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, is an AI architecture that improves language-model responses by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and supplying it to the model as contextual evidence.
introduction: RAG connects large language models with private, current or domain-specific information. Instead of relying entirely on knowledge learned during training, the model receives relevant source material at request time and uses it to produce a more grounded response.

seo.title: What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
seo.description: Learn how retrieval-augmented generation works, its core components, benefits, limitations and practical applications in enterprise AI systems.

sections.title: How retrieval-augmented generation works
sections.description: A RAG system combines information retrieval with language generation in a controlled pipeline.

content.text: When a user submits a question, the system first converts that question into a numerical representation known as an embedding. It then compares the embedding with indexed content stored inside a search system or vector database.

content.title: A typical RAG request follows these stages:
items: The user submits a question or instruction.
The system converts the request into an embedding or searchable query.
The retrieval layer finds the most relevant documents or passages.
Optional filtering and re-ranking improve the quality of the retrieved context.
The selected context and original question are sent to the language model.
The language model generates a response grounded in the supplied information.
The application may return citations, source links or confidence information with the answer.

content.title: The central idea
content.text: The language model does not need to permanently memorize every piece of business knowledge. Relevant information can be retrieved and supplied when it is needed.

sections.title: Core components of a RAG system

items.label: Knowledge sources
items.value: Documents, databases, websites, APIs, support tickets, policies and other trusted information.

items.label: Ingestion pipeline
items.value: Processes that collect, clean, divide and prepare source content for retrieval.

items.label: Embedding model
items.value: Transforms text or other content into numerical vectors that represent semantic meaning.

items.label: Retrieval system
items.value: Searches indexed content and identifies passages that are relevant to the user request.

items.label: Re-ranking layer
items.value: Reorders retrieved results so the strongest evidence is placed closest to the model.

items.label: Language model
items.value: Uses the retrieved context to generate a useful, natural-language response.

content.title: Best suited for
content.text: RAG is especially valuable when answers must reflect changing, proprietary or highly specialized information.

RAG does not automatically guarantee accurate answers. The generated response still depends on the quality of the source content, chunking strategy, retrieval method, ranking logic, prompt construction and language model.

items: Poor source data can produce poor retrieved context.
Large or badly designed chunks may reduce retrieval precision.
Relevant evidence can be missed when queries are ambiguous.
Retrieved passages may contain conflicting or outdated information.
Additional retrieval stages can increase latency and infrastructure cost.
Permissions must be enforced before private information reaches the model.
The model may still misinterpret correctly retrieved evidence.

content.title: Important
content.text: A production RAG system requires evaluation of both retrieval quality and generated-answer quality. Measuring only the final response can hide weaknesses inside the retrieval pipeline.

sections.title: When should an organization use RAG?

content.text: RAG is a strong option when an application needs information that is private, frequently updated, too large to place permanently in a prompt or outside the model’s original training knowledge.

content.title: Consider RAG when:
items: Answers must use internal company information.
Users need citations or supporting evidence.
The knowledge base changes regularly.
Different users have different data-access permissions.
The application covers a specialized professional domain.
The team needs to update knowledge without retraining a model.

content.title: RAG is not always required
content.text: For simple writing, summarization or transformation tasks where all necessary information is already provided in the prompt, a retrieval system may add unnecessary complexity.

items.question: What does RAG stand for in artificial intelligence?
items.answer: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It describes a system that retrieves relevant external information and supplies it to a generative model before the model creates its response.

items.question: Does RAG train or fine-tune the language model?
items.answer: Not necessarily. A standard RAG pipeline retrieves information at request time and places it in the model context. Fine-tuning can be used alongside RAG, but it is a separate technique.

items.question: Does a RAG system always require a vector database?
items.answer: No. Vector databases are common because they support semantic retrieval, but a RAG system can also use keyword search, relational databases, graph databases, APIs or a hybrid combination of retrieval methods.

items.question: Can RAG completely prevent hallucinations?
items.answer: No. Strong retrieval and prompting can reduce unsupported responses, but the model may still ignore, misunderstand or incorrectly combine retrieved evidence. Evaluation and guardrails remain necessary.

items.question: What is hybrid retrieval in RAG?
items.answer: Hybrid retrieval combines multiple search methods, commonly semantic vector search and keyword search. This can improve performance when queries contain both conceptual meaning and important exact terms.
